truth_notice.en: These are newly authored StreetGym replacement sessions.

description.en: Build on the Level 1 pull-overs while strict pulling and squats stay honest.
Build steady dip strength, balanced legs, and a quiet support position.
Practice the inverted tuck without fatigue, then reinforce the trunk.
Connect the pull, transition, and support with deliberate low-bar practice.
A straightforward strength day keeps every major pattern in the week.
Four unhurried rounds mix bar control, pushing, legs, and playful movement.
Walk, restore shoulder range, and lengthen hips before the next build day.
Slow lowering turns each pull-over into controlled strength instead of momentum.
A controlled rep staircase strengthens the press while legs supply balance.
Find a stable inverted tuck, then explore small controlled directions.
Separate pull, turnover, and press before linking the whole bar transition.
Alternating submaximal sets builds useful volume without sacrificing clean repetitions.
Move through five stations at a conversational pace and leave one round unused.
Gentle loading and longer mobility restore the joints used around the bar.
Use fewer repetitions to prove that the pull-over is smooth in both directions.
Short pauses sharpen dip and push-up positions during a low-volume day.
A light bodyline session links inversion, hollow shape, and easy rowing.
Rehearse crisp low-bar transitions and finish each repetition in stable support.
Small clusters preserve speed and form while revisiting every essential movement.
Rotate through short stations and make every repetition look the same.
A gentle review records control without turning the final day into a max test. Clean reps up to the number shown: stop at the first form break and note it; don't top up with the easier option.
Explosive but tidy pulls begin the next phase without abandoning strict strength.
Stable support and full dips prepare the press above a single bar.
Small hollow-to-arch swings teach bar rhythm while inversion work stays easy.
High pulls and low-bar turnovers meet before a calm straight-bar finish.
Antagonist pairs deliver useful basics while keeping every set below failure.
A lively station circuit changes the order while the familiar basics remain.
Easy walking and shoulder control absorb the first week of power practice.
Crisp singles raise pulling height before moderate strict-pull volume.
Strong bar pressing alternates with unilateral leg work for an athletic session.
Long rests keep hollow-arch rhythm precise and shoulders comfortable.
Create speed below the bar and stillness above it in separated drills.
Alternating sets add basic volume while preserving two clean repetitions in reserve.
A varied circuit mixes rowing, support travel, lunges, and trunk control.
A longer recovery flow restores wrists, shoulders, spine, hips, and ankles.
Low volume and full rest reveal whether pulling height is truly controlled.
Paused support and presses check bar stability with fresh shoulders.
Easy shapes, partial inversions and a few tuck front-lever rows consolidate rhythm without adding fatigue.
A short rehearsal links speed, turnover, and support without chasing fatigue.
Moderate sets audit clean pull-ups, dips, push-ups, squats, and raises before the source workouts begin.
An easy re-entry after the source workouts: a playful low-effort mix of rows, bar walks, squats and presses that repeats none of their circuits.
Walking, gentle hanging, and full-body mobility prepare the first assisted muscle-up week.
Low-rep assisted muscle-ups introduce the full path while strict pulls remain central.
Pressing above the bar grows alongside steady push-ups and single-leg strength.
Front-lever tuck holds and back-lever tuck entries share a calm technique session; a feet-supported German hang opens the shoulders before the entries.
Alternate band and jump assistance to understand one consistent muscle-up path.
A traditional strength session supports the new skill with dependable foundations.
Five playful stations revisit support, rowing, bodyline, legs, and balance.
Low-intensity mobility and walking restore range after the first muscle-up week.
Use the least assistance that preserves a fast pull and symmetrical turnover.
Three pressing angles stack into one session while supported pistol squats keep the base strong.
Alternate front tuck holds with back-lever tuck entries so neither straight-arm pattern dominates.
Slow muscle-up descents map the transition while explosive pulls stay sharp.

A small pyramid makes familiar basics engaging without asking for failure. Today the basics are one recorded set each, a little above your best so far. Clean reps up to the number shown: stop at the first form break and note it; don't top up with the easier option.
A flowing five-movement circuit blends bars, floor, legs, and trunk.
Longer mobility and easy bodyline holds restore shape between harder weeks.
A deload keeps the assisted path symmetrical and leaves the elbows fresh.
Brief holds and paused presses verify support quality at reduced volume.
Feet-supported hangs and a short German hang keep the shoulders open while lever holds rest; tuck L-sits keep the trunk working.
A few high-quality transitions show the current path without accumulating fatigue.
Five moderate basics maintain strength while the skill block unloads.
Easy stations add novelty while keeping breathing and technique under control.
A long walk and joint care prepare the move toward cleaner, lighter assistance.
Complete the band muscle-ups and slow negatives before the listed basics; use the jump regression for any uneven band rep. Strict singles begin in Level 3.
Straight-bar pressing and stable support make the top of every transition reliable.
Accumulate short perfect tuck holds instead of chasing one shaky maximum.
Chest-to-bar pulls, band muscle-ups and slow negatives build the transition while strict pulling stays crisp; strict singles begin in Level 3.

Ascending basics build capacity while every top set retains clean form. Today the basics are one recorded set each, a little above your best so far. Clean reps up to the number shown: stop at the first form break and note it; don't top up with the easier option.
Follow a varied trail from rows to support, legs, crawling, and trunk control.
Walking, light scapular work, and mobility unload the elbows after clean attempts.
Widely spaced singles develop a repeatable muscle-up without grinding.
Bar dips and pike push-ups strengthen two pressing directions with balanced legs.
Slightly longer lever holds build patience while rows reinforce position.
Break the hard-day run with assisted, low-volume turnover practice. Leave several reps in reserve and treat every set as technique.
Pull, push, legs, and trunk receive equal attention in a steady session.
Alternate bar and floor stations for a lively session that never becomes frantic.
Gentle movement and long breathing lower fatigue before the final build week.
A few fresh singles assess symmetry; assisted reps replace every doubtful attempt.
Paused bar and parallel dips verify depth, lockout, and shoulder comfort.
Short front and back holds capture progress without testing shaky limits.
Compare low-bar, assisted, and clean transition paths at deliberately low volume.
Submaximal benchmark sets confirm that skill practice has not displaced the basics.
Easy movement puzzles keep the habit enjoyable while fatigue continues to fall.
A restorative review records readiness for the final Level 2 bridge.
Bank several rested muscle-up singles, then reinforce strict pulling strength.
Build dip capacity while deliberately stopping two repetitions before failure.
Solid tuck holds and controlled rows prepare the lever work awaiting in Level 3.
Interrupt the loading streak with easy assisted transitions, quiet supports, and submaximal basics that restore crisp movement.
Strong submaximal basics verify that advanced practice rests on a broad base.
A varied circuit challenges control and stamina without repeating a prior session.
Long walking and gentle mobility create room for the final bridge week.
Rehearse four clean muscle-ups only if the first pair remains effortless and even.
Full lockouts above both bar types build confidence for repeated transitions.
Tuck holds and partial skin-the-cat control prepare safe lever lowering.
Use the fourth day to restore turnover timing at low intensity, keeping assistance generous and every repetition comfortably submaximal.
Strong but nonmaximal basics establish the reserve needed for demanding Level 3 days.
A fresh movement order keeps the final bridge playful and technically light.
A deliberately easy day restores the body before five separate readiness checks.
Pass with ten strict pull-ups, three chest-high pulls, and three controlled pull-overs; otherwise repeat the bridge.
Pass twelve parallel dips, eight bar dips, twenty push-ups, and thirty clean squats.
Rehearse below maximum and record whether the original markers - a twenty-second tuck L-sit and controlled ten-second front and back tucks - feel available. Do not test to failure today.

Complete one set of four muscle-ups, then two sets of two, 2x8 bar dips, 2x6 pull-ups, and two thirty-second hollow holds. Use each listed regression for any unclean set; this is one required check in the collective sequence.

Complete the prescribed recovery, then continue to the next assigned program only when every Level 2 check is clean. If any check is not clean, repeat the preceding bridge with its listed regressions and then repeat the complete check block.
Begin the next skill block by resetting volume to roughly sixty percent. Keep every technique dose easy and stop well before fatigue.
Front-lever holds and rows develop straight-arm control without rushing extension.
Gentle planche leans join strong dips, push-ups, and unilateral legs.
Walking and a full joint flow restore the body between three skill directions.
Muscle-up singles, pulls, and dips share volume without any maximal set.
Bent-knee negatives introduce the flag while hollow work protects the bodyline.
A low-pressure sequence connects a supported back-lever entry, tuck front lever, crawling, and balanced legs.
Repeat clean muscle-up pairs with full rest and finish with ordinary pulling.
Back-lever entries and holds build shoulder control while rows balance the session.
Planche leans and deep presses develop forward support without skipping leg work.
A long walk and gentle joint work absorb the week's straight-arm loading.

Submaximal pulling and dipping protect the basic strength behind advanced skills. Today the basics are one recorded set each, a little above your best so far. Clean reps up to the number shown: stop at the first form break and note it; don't top up with the easier option.
Longer bent-knee descents strengthen the flag line while avoiding forced full-body holds.
Short front- and back-lever stations plus straight-bar support keep muscle-up top-position strength in the sequence at controlled intensity.
Brief advanced-tuck attempts follow solid tuck holds and stop before the hips drop.
Muscle-up pairs and bar dips strengthen every position above the turnover.
Measure forward lean through shoulder position, never by collapsing the lower back.
Visit wrists, shoulders, spine, hips, and ankles in an unhurried recovery flow.
Short clusters increase useful muscle-up density while full rest protects technique.
A controlled eccentric ladder adds time under tension without forcing full flags.
Close the week with easy fundamentals and a supported back-lever entry, restoring movement quality before the next three-day skill wave.
Rows strengthen the tuck line before a few careful advanced-tuck holds.
Perform two sets of three and three sets of two with at least two reps in reserve; use the listed band regression for any set that is not clean.
Balance and forward lean share wrist-friendly sets with ordinary pressing.
Easy walking, mobility, and breathing reduce stiffness before another bar day.
Tuck back-lever holds follow controlled entries, with no forced shoulder depth.
Dragon negatives lead, then familiar push-ups, squats, and rows complete the day.
Sample each developing skill lightly and finish wanting one more round.
Strong advanced-tuck holds, tuck L-sits and rows build the line a one-leg lever will need later; return to the tuck if the hips turn.
Skin-the-cat, tuck entries and arch holds build shoulder-extension tolerance; longer back-lever shapes wait until the entries stay smooth.
Forward leans pair with strong pressing while wrist comfort controls the range.
A long easy walk and gentle mobility restore the spine, shoulders, wrists, and hips.
Perform three sets of three and three sets of two while every rep stays fast; use the listed band regression at the first slow or uneven repetition.
Slow bent-knee descents advance the dragon flag while the trunk stays rigid.
End the week with deliberately easy regressions for pull, dip, push, squat, and core so the next progression wave begins recovered.
Alternating holds and rows make the advanced tuck stronger without forcing longer shapes.
Slow tuck entries and skin-the-cat lowering develop control; holds return only while the shoulders stay comfortable.
Balance, forward lean, and pressing create a varied planche foundation without wrist strain.
An easy day restores shoulder extension, spinal rotation, hips, and wrists between lever sessions.
Complete a submaximal 2-3-3-2 ladder; at the first slow or uneven rep, use the listed band regression for every remaining rung.
Front-lever rows, tuck back-lever holds and bent-knee dragon negatives share trunk work without maximal holds.
Use easy regressions and short movement-quality sets across the park to break the loading streak while retaining every fundamental pattern.

Band-assisted muscle-ups, ten-rep pull-ups, advanced-tuck front holds, tuck rows and hanging leg raises bridge to Level 4; the first strict muscle-up waits for the next readiness check. Use each listed regression at the first form break.
Strong dips and controlled planche leans prepare the next level without sacrificing legs.

Complete one set of five muscle-ups, one set of three, one set of ten pull-ups, and 2x8 bar dips with one or two reps in reserve. Use each listed regression at the first form break; this is one required part of the collective Level 3 check.
Two easy technique sets per pattern preserve the basics while fatigue falls before testing.
Advanced-tuck front holds, tuck back holds and dragon negatives connect the three bodyline goals before Level 4.

Complete 1x15 parallel dips, 1x10 bar dips, 1x25 push-ups, 1x40 squats, and the assigned eight-second planche lean. Use each listed regression for any unclean step; all five are required in the collective check.

Complete one ten-second advanced front tuck, one twelve-second tuck back lever, one set of three dragon negatives per side, one twenty-five-second tuck L-sit, and two thirty-five-second hollow holds. Use each listed regression if a step is not clean; this result joins the prior checks to progress the sequence.

Complete the assigned recovery, then continue to the next program only when every Level 3 readiness check is clean. If any check is not clean, repeat the preceding bridge with the listed regressions and then repeat the complete check block.
